I preliminary checked the issue. There is talk about book entry adjustments in the process of moving funds from one account to the next, from one project to the next, etc.

For those having no bookkeeping skills allow me to shed some light on the proceeding:

Consider bookkeeping as having a cabinet with several drawers. Each drawer has a number. Say, number 0001 to 9999. That is almost 10.000 drawers.

There are groupings of drawers as well. Let's assign them a color code. Fixed assets like land, buildings, investments etc are colored bright red. Cash and cashinstruments like bankaccounts, checks, money orders, and what have you, bright yellow.

There is accounts receivable in bright orange. What is in stock, think of vehicles, planes, tanks, weapons, munitions, scopes, helmets, boots, rations, etc, or what is in the warehouses across the world is in color green.

Accounts payable in bright blue, long term loans in pitch black, taxes in pink, and equity in bright white.

We just have all these bright colors grouped because they belong on a balance sheet.

For the profit and loss ( p&L) all kinds of drawers are colored in softcover: operating income, like money received from Congress, contributions from other countries, sale of out of date stock, etc, and of operating costs like reservations, depreciations, insurance, interest paid, salaries, contributions, memberships, etc etc.

Normally, when I go audit books, I always find unaplied cash. Both on the accounts receivable as on the accounts payable. I find invoices that cannot be applied to an order, open orders never applied to invoices, there are many reasons for making entry mistakes that result in unapplied.

So, if we only take the mistake of booking of a to be paid invoice of 1000 dollar value under accounts receivable instead of account payable, what does that mean?

For one, we have a 2000 dollar difference. Because in simple view: instead of +1000, we have to have had -1000. Here plus is the debit side, and minus the credit side.

Note however that when the bank credits your account, it views this act from the vantage point of the bank: the bank owes you that money, hence a credit.

We already spoke about order. Let s just say there is an order for rations. The order is made invoices come in and are applied to this order. Every invoice signifies as delivery. Every delivery is going to a warehouse. A warehouse is divided into sections that exactly register what delivery should be stocked right there.

Ever expected a delivery that never showed up and got lost in process? Or ever received something you did not order? Or that your delivery is delivered at a different address?

Many things can go wrong and each has it's own remedial action and registry as a book entry.

Let's just say that over the last 50 years, the pentagon has had an appropriation of on average 400 billion. That is 20T in total.

In bookkeeping an order creation leads to at least 2 entries:

A debit and a credit entry. :

Orders project x debit.

Invoices to be received. credit

When the invoice is received:

Accounts payable credit

Invoices to be received debit

Usually there is an approval process. So let's add that in, so when an invoice.is received:

Invoices to be approved credit

Invoices to be received debit

When the invoice.is approved :

Invoice to be approved debit

Accounts payable credit.

Then we plug in the payment:

Accounts payable debit

Bankaccount credit.

As you can see this simple process requires an entry for every status of an invoice. Mistakes are made. And when a small company often looks at unapplied running up to 10.000 and in some case I have seen several million, and this is really either double/ triple paid by the debtor, or double triple paid by the company itself, what do you think 20T will get you with.thousands of warehouses, millions of invoices, hundreds of thousands of items, soldiers, salaries, you name it.

Billions of entries. And when we apply a margin of error of only. 0.1%, that is every 1000 entries is a mistake, we are taking millions of mistakes. Some mistakes concern small figures, others sometimes run in the tens if not hundreds of thousand. The sheer volume makes it difficult to reconcile.

Every mistake at least counts.double as two entries at least are tight up in the mistake. And as I have shown with the example of the wrongly debit booked invoice instead of credit: the amount doubles as well.

As I said in my previous post: the sheer finding that 35T needs reconciliation, does not mean that amount is drawn out of the pentagon. Merely, it is the total sum of all mistakes in bookentries.

Now, it may be that some concerns misplaced nuclear bombs, submarines and toaster ovens. or simply petty cash that has gone missing, or rations that fell of the truck, whatever.

But it is not what you were thinking. And, as I showed you with the margin of error, the pentagon may be doing a better job at bookkeeping than many give them credit for. And yes, some accountants love cooking the books. Very easy to do. And if you know how to look, easy to spot.
